blk_part_01_part_1_a_famous_mushroom_of_.text: The white spots also have a story. When the mushroom is young, a protective layer called a veil covers it. As the cap grows, the veil breaks, and the white spots are pieces that stay behind. Rain can wash them away, so some fly agarics have no spots at all. This is one reason why colour and spots are not a reliable way to judge a mushroom.

It was a kind of insecticide, a substance that kills insects. Notice what the name tells us and what it does not tell us. It shows that people found a practical use for the mushroom. However, it does not show that they ate it. In fact, eating it can cause hallucinations and painful stomach cramps.

blk_part_02_part_2_who_actually_ate_it_a.text: In northern Eurasia, especially Siberia, several groups used the fly agaric. These included the Nenets, Yukaghir, Koryak and Chukchi peoples. Their reasons were different. Sometimes they used it for fun and relaxation, and sometimes they used it in rituals. The mushroom could create dream-like experiences. Some people believed that, during these experiences, they met their ancestors or spirits. This was their belief and part of their way of understanding the world. It is not a scientific fact about the mushroom.

blk_part_03_part_3_ibotenic_acid_and_mus.text: To understand muscimol, think about how the brain sends messages. Brain cells talk to each other with chemical messages. Each message needs a receptor, a receiving place on a cell, like a lock that accepts only certain keys. One important messenger is called GABA. GABA usually tells brain cells to calm down and send fewer signals, a bit like a brake in a car. Muscimol acts on GABA-A receptors, so it pushes on this braking system.

blk_part_04_part_4_is_it_a_magic_mushroo.text: This leads to a clear answer. In a broad sense, both mushrooms are psychoactive, which means they change how the mind works and how people see the world. Because of that shared effect, it makes cultural sense to talk about them together, for example in history or in stories. But it does not make scientific sense to treat them as the same thing. The fly agaric is not a psilocybin mushroom. Its chemicals are different, they act in a different way, and one cannot replace the other.
